concept_html:
A Power BI semantic model works best on a star schema: fact tables surrounded by dimension tables. Microsoft's Power BI guidance (checked September 2026) defines the parts:

  • Fact tables store observations or events: survey responses, orders, balances. They hold dimension key columns and numeric measure columns. The dimension keys decide the fact table's grain, for example one row per respondent per wave per brand.
  • Dimension tables describe business entities: respondent, brand, region, date. Each has a unique key column and descriptive columns used to filter and group. A date dimension belongs in almost every model.

Relationships run one-to-many from each dimension to the fact table, and filters flow from the dimension to the fact. Microsoft recommends that you minimise bi-directional relationships, which can slow queries and confuse report users with unexpected filtering. Many-to-many relationships between facts and dimensions usually mean the grain is unclear.

Build the star in the gold layer, not in the model:

  • Compute derived columns such as age bands or weighted flags in Spark or SQL, in gold tables. Direct Lake on SQL analytics endpoints does not support calculated columns, and on OneLake they are in preview with restrictions. Materialised calculated columns in Import models slow refresh.
  • Give every fact table a clear grain in its docstring and table comment (lesson A2-L3).
  • Use surrogate or natural keys consistently, and check they are unique in each dimension (lesson C2-L2 showed warehouse keys are not enforced).

A good model is boring: one fact table per grain, conformed dimensions shared between facts, single-direction one-to-many relationships, and measures that do the arithmetic (lesson C6-L2).

exercises.prompt:
Write `model_warnings(relationships: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[str]` for a model review. Each relationship has `from_table`, `to_table`, `cardinality` (`"one_to_many"` or `"many_to_many"`) and `direction` (`"single"` or `"both"`). Return, in input order, a warning for each problem:

- `"<from>-<to>: many-to-many"` for a many-to-many relationship,
- `"<from>-<to>: bi-directional"` for direction both.

A relationship with both problems produces both warnings, many-to-many first.
exercises.prompt_html:
Write model_warnings(relationships: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[str] for a model review. Each relationship has from_table, to_table, cardinality ("one_to_many" or "many_to_many") and direction ("single" or "both"). Return, in input order, a warning for each problem:

  • "<from>-<to>: many-to-many" for a many-to-many relationship,
  • "<from>-<to>: bi-directional" for direction both.

A relationship with both problems produces both warnings, many-to-many first.
exercises.solution:
def model_warnings(relationships: list[dict[str, str]]) -> list[str]:
    """Warnings for relationships that break star-schema guidance.

    Args:
        relationships: Dicts with from_table, to_table, cardinality and direction.

    Returns:
        Warning strings in input order.
    """
    warnings = []
    for rel in relationships:
        name = f"{rel['from_table']}-{rel['to_table']}"
        if rel["cardinality"] == "many_to_many":
            warnings.append(f"{name}: many-to-many")
        if rel["direction"] == "both":
            warnings.append(f"{name}: bi-directional")
    return warnings

title: Star schemas for semantic models
why_html: A brand tracker model joined a respondent table and a brand-awareness table with a bi-directional many-to-many relationship, because both held respondent_id and brand. Selecting a brand in a slicer filtered respondents, which filtered back to every brand those respondents had mentioned. Awareness for small brands showed as much higher than the survey measured. A single fact table at respondent-brand grain with one-way dimensions returned the correct figures.
